notes: The hosted main form int main(void) works in all the course's language modes. C99 and later define reaching the end of main as returning zero. C17 remains the build baseline here; do not replace main's int return type with void based on old compiler-specific examples.

examQuestions.question: Explain the roles of stdio.h, main and return 0 in Hello World.
examQuestions.answerHtml: stdio.h declares standard I/O facilities such as printf. In a hosted program, main is the entry function; int main(void) takes no arguments and returns an int status. return 0 reports successful termination and does not print a zero.

examQuestions.question: Explain the build and execution of Hello World and identify three common first-day source mistakes.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
The compiler checks and translates saved source, and linking connects required library code before execution begins. At runtime main calls printf to write the string, then returns a success status. A missing semicolon breaks the statement grammar, incorrect quote delimiters fail to form the intended string, and Printf does not name the declared lowercase printf function. Read the earliest diagnostic, repair the source and rebuild before testing the result.

Marking: build versus run 2, three diagnosed mistakes 3.

examQuestions.question: Write a complete C program for this lab task: Read two scores, each 0 to 100; output Input: then First: A, Second: B, Total: S on three lines.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int first, second;
    printf("Input: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d", &first, &second) != 2) {
        return 1;
    }
    printf("First: %d\nSecond: %d\nTotal: %d\n", first, second, first + second);
    return 0;
}

Marking: 1 for typed declarations, 1 for checked input, 2 for the required calculation or transformation, and 1 for exact output.
